# OSB strand dryer dataset — data dictionary

Synthetic dataset for OEE (Overall Equipment Effectiveness) analysis of oriented
strand board (OSB) strand dryers.

**This data is synthetic.** It is generated by `generate_osb_dryer_data.py` from
published industry figures. It contains no proprietary or employer-internal
information from any company. Parameters were chosen to be representative of a
mid-sized North American OSB mill; they do not describe any specific facility.

---

## Process background

OSB is made by flaking small-diameter logs into thin strands, drying those
strands, blending them with resin and wax, forming them into a mat, and pressing
the mat into panels. The **strand dryer** sits between the flaker and the
blender. Green strands enter at high moisture content and must leave within a
narrow target band — published sources put finished strand moisture content at
roughly 3–7%.

That narrow band is why a dryer is an interesting OEE subject. Under-dried
strands cause blows and blisters at the press. Over-dried strands break down
into fines, lose yield, and raise fire risk. The equipment can be running at
full speed and still be producing loss.

A dryer is **continuous process equipment**, not discrete. There is no unit
count, so throughput is measured in bone-dry tons (BDT) — the mass of wood
excluding water.

---

## Files

| File | Grain | Source system it represents |
|---|---|---|
| `osb_dryer_shifts.csv` | one row per date × shift × dryer | PLC / historian |
| `osb_downtime_events.csv` | one row per logged stop | operator-entered downtime log |

The two files **do not reconcile exactly**, by design. See "Known data quality
issues" below.

---

## `osb_dryer_shifts.csv`

| Column | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Date` | date | Production date, ISO format |
| `Shift` | text | `Day` or `Night` (12-hour shifts) |
| `Dryer_ID` | text | `DRYER_1` or `DRYER_2` |
| `Planned_Time_Min` | int | Minutes the dryer was scheduled to run. Normally 720. Reduced for planned maintenance and market curtailment. |
| `Downtime_Min` | int | Unplanned stopped time. Equipment fault, process upset, or safety trip. |
| `Blocked_Starved_Min` | int | Time stopped because an **adjacent** operation stopped. Starved = no furnish from the green end. Blocked = dry bin full because the press is down. The dryer itself was healthy. |
| `Ideal_Rate_BDT_Hr` | float | Nameplate throughput in bone-dry tons per hour. |
| `Output_BDT` | float | Total bone-dry tons discharged from the dryer. |
| `Rework_BDT` | float | Output outside the target moisture band that must be re-dried. Recoverable, but consumes future capacity. |
| `Fines_BDT` | float | Output degraded to fines by over-drying. Not recoverable as product; typically diverted to fuel. |

**Good output** = `Output_BDT − Rework_BDT − Fines_BDT`.

`Rework_BDT` and `Fines_BDT` are separated deliberately. Collapsing them into a
single "defects" column would lose the distinction between a recoverable
throughput cost and a permanent yield loss, which are different problems with
different fixes.

## `osb_downtime_events.csv`

| Column | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Event_ID` | int | Surrogate key |
| `Date`, `Shift`, `Dryer_ID` | | Join keys back to the shift table |
| `Reason` | text | Free-ish text reason code as selected by the operator |
| `Category` | text | `Mechanical`, `Electrical`, `Process`, `Fire/Safety`, `Changeover`, `Blocked`, `Starved` |
| `Duration_Min` | int | Duration as reported by the operator |

---

## Parameter derivation

Every number below traces to a published figure.

**Nameplate dryer rate.** Published North American OSB mill capacities run
roughly 400–860 million square feet per year on a 3/8-inch basis. This dataset
assumes a 600 MMSF/yr mill.

```
1 MSF (3/8-in basis)        = 0.885 m³
OSB panel density           ≈ 640 kg/m³
                            → 0.624 short tons of panel per MSF

600,000 MSF/yr × 0.624      = 374,600 tons/yr of finished panel
less ~5% moisture, ~4% resin and wax
                            = 340,900 oven-dry tons of wood in panel
divided by ~88% yield downstream of the dryer
  (screening fines, forming and trim, sanding)
                            = 387,400 BDT/yr leaving the dryers
over ~8,000 scheduled hours = 48.4 BDT/hr for the mill
over 2 dryers               = 24.2 BDT/hr average required
```

Nameplate must exceed the required average, so the dryers are set at **26.0 and
29.0 BDT/hr**. Two different rates is intentional: it means you cannot compare
raw `Output_BDT` between dryers without normalizing, which is the whole reason
performance is expressed as a ratio.

**Moisture content and quality losses.** Target strand MC of 3–7% is published.
Rework and fines rates are not consistently published, so they are modeled at
roughly 2–4% and 1–2% of output respectively, which lands overall quality in the
95–97% range typical of continuous process equipment.

**Availability and performance** are tuned so that headline OEE lands in the
mid-60s to high-70s depending on how blocked/starved time is treated. Published
guidance puts "world class" discrete OEE near 85% and typical plants at 60–80%.

### Sources

- U.S. EPA, *AP-42 Section 10.6.1, Waferboard/Oriented Strandboard Manufacturing* — process description, oven-dried ton basis
- Canadian Wood Council, *Oriented Strand Board (OSB) Manufacture* — 3–7% target strand moisture content, resin and wax loadings
- Forisk, *OSB Mill Capacity in North America* — sector capacity and wood consumption
- Published mill capacity announcements (Norbord High Level 860 MMSF, West Fraser 550 MMSF, Norbord Cordele 400+ MMSF) — mill size range
- *BioResources*, "Oriented strand board: Opportunities and potential products in China" — 1,000 ft² (3/8-in basis) = 0.885 m³

---

## Known data quality issues

These are **intentional**. They are the conditions you actually meet in a plant,
and handling them is most of the analytical work.

1. **Unaccounted downtime.** The operator event log captures only about 75–80%
   of the stopped time the PLC recorded. Long stops are logged reliably. Stops
   under 15 minutes are logged inconsistently, and micro-stops under 5 minutes
   are almost never logged. Summing the event log will understate downtime.
   Deciding what to do with the gap is a judgment call you have to make and
   document.

2. **Operator rounding.** Reported durations in the event log are rounded to the
   nearest 5 minutes. Expect a spike at multiples of 5 in any duration
   histogram.

3. **Blocked/starved time is not equipment failure.** Whether it counts against
   dryer availability is a definitional choice, not a fact. Counting it moves
   headline OEE by about 4 points. Whichever you pick, state it plainly in your
   README — an OEE figure without its definition attached is not a number.

4. **`Planned_Time_Min` varies.** Do not hardcode 720. Planned maintenance
   windows and a market curtailment period in May reduce it. Hardcoding will
   silently inflate availability on exactly the shifts where it matters.

---

## OEE formulas

```
Run_Time      = Planned_Time_Min − Downtime_Min [− Blocked_Starved_Min]
Availability  = Run_Time / Planned_Time_Min
Performance   = Output_BDT / (Ideal_Rate_BDT_Hr × Run_Time / 60)
Quality       = (Output_BDT − Rework_BDT − Fines_BDT) / Output_BDT
OEE           = Availability × Performance × Quality
```

Guard the denominators. Shifts exist where `Run_Time` or `Output_BDT` is zero.
